title: Planning Narratives
keyIdea: Plan a story by borrowing methods from a mentor text, not its words. Show a character through action, speech and thought instead of naming the trait, choose setting details that build one mood, and move from a wide view to a close-up to build suspense.

kid: Good writers read like writers. They pick a book they love and ask: how did the author do that? That book is a mentor text. You borrow the method, not the words.

One method is show, don't tell. Telling names the feeling: Sam was nervous. Showing lets the reader work it out: Sam folded the note, then unfolded it. Plan what your character does, says and thinks. Do not plan the word nervous.

A setting is more than where the story happens. It sets a mood. A gate that creaks and a window that goes dark make us uneasy. Bright sun and kids on swings make us calm. Pick details that all build the same mood.

Some authors zoom in like a camera. They start wide, with the whole valley. Then the lane. Then the door. Then one spider on the knocker. Each line gets closer, and the reader leans in. Put these notes in your plan before you write.
adult: This topic is about planning a story before drafting, using a mentor text as a model. Learners study how a published author reveals a character or builds a setting, then use the same method in a plan of their own. The aim is to copy the craft, not the sentences.

In the lab, learners sort lines into telling and showing and label a short mentor paragraph by method: action, speech, thought or looks. They then plan a new character through three notes and choose setting details that build an uneasy mood. Last, they order lines from a wide view to a close-up.

Common mistakes: naming the trait in the plan, such as brave, so the draft just tells; adding very instead of a detail; mixing cheerful and creepy details so the mood is lost; and copying the mentor's sentences instead of its method. A plan made only of plot events, with no notes on character or setting, is another mistake to watch for.

Check the plan, not just the story. Each character note should be something seen or heard, and each setting note should fit the chosen mood. Learners at this age often find it easier to plan in short notes than in full sentences.

familyTip: Read the first page of a favourite book together. Ask: how do we know what this character is like, without being told? Then plan one new character using the same trick.

practice.prompt: Which line shows that Ben is angry, instead of telling us?
choices: Ben was really angry.
Ben slammed his bag on the table and said nothing.
Ben felt anger inside him.
practice.hint: Look for an action the reader can picture, with no feeling word.
practice.explain: Slamming the bag is an action. The reader works out that Ben is angry, so the line shows it. The other two name the feeling.

practice.prompt: In a mentor text, Mia checks the clock {n} times in one minute. What is the author showing?
choices: That Mia is calm and relaxed
That the clock is broken
That Mia is worried or impatient
practice.hint: Why would someone keep looking at a clock?
practice.explain: Checking the clock {n} times is an action that shows worry or impatience. The author never names the feeling, so the reader works it out.

practice.prompt: You want an uneasy mood outside an old house. Which detail fits best?
choices: A door creaks open, but no one is there.
Birds sing in the sunny garden.
The house was very spooky.
practice.hint: Pick a detail you can hear or see, not a word that names the mood.
practice.explain: A creaking door with no one there makes the reader uneasy. Birds singing fights the mood, and very spooky just tells it.

practice.prompt: Your setting plan has {n} creepy details and one cheerful one. What should you do?
choices: Add more cheerful details to balance it
Cut or change the cheerful detail so every note builds the same mood
Keep it, because more details are always better
practice.hint: What is the job of each setting detail?
practice.explain: Every detail should build the one mood you chose. One cheerful note among {n} creepy ones breaks the spell, so cut it or change it.

practice.prompt: A mentor text zooms in. Which order goes from wide to close-up?
choices: A tear on her cheek, her face, the crowded hall
Her face, the crowded hall, a tear on her cheek
The crowded hall, her face, a tear on her cheek
practice.hint: Start with the biggest view and end with the smallest detail.
practice.explain: A camera zoom starts wide, the crowded hall, then moves to her face, then to one tear. Each step is closer than the last.

choices: A book you copy word for word
A text you study to borrow an author's methods
A list of spelling rules
pool.hint: Think of a mentor as someone you learn from.
pool.explain: A mentor text is one you study to learn how an author did something, such as show a character, then use that method in your own words.

pool.prompt: Which plan note shows that Lola is shy?
choices: Lola is shy.
Lola is very, very shy.
Lola hides behind her book when the teacher asks a question.
pool.hint: Look for something the reader could picture.
pool.explain: Hiding behind a book is an action that shows shyness. The other notes tell the trait, and adding very still tells.

pool.prompt: A character says, “I'm fine,” but thinks, “I want to go home.” What does the gap show?
choices: That the character is hiding a feeling
That the character is lying for fun
Nothing, because speech always tells the truth
pool.hint: Compare what is said with what is thought.
pool.explain: When speech and thought do not match, the reader sees a hidden feeling. Authors use this gap to show, not tell.

pool.prompt: Which method is used here: “Her coat was two sizes too big and patched at the elbows”?
choices: Speech
Looks
Thought
pool.hint: Is this something she says, thinks, or how she appears?
pool.explain: It describes how she appears, so the method is looks. It hints that her family may not have much money.

pool.prompt: Your character waits {n} minutes at the bus stop. Which note best shows he is bored?
choices: He was bored.
He counts the cracks in the pavement, then counts them again.
He is very bored.
pool.hint: Pick what he does, not a feeling word.
pool.explain: Counting cracks twice is an action that shows boredom. After {n} minutes the reader can feel it too, without the word bored.

pool.prompt: You loved how a mentor text zooms in on a spider. How should you use it?
choices: Copy the spider sentence word for word
Zoom in on a different detail in your own setting
Skip it, because borrowing is cheating
pool.hint: Borrow the method, not the words.
pool.explain: Copying the sentence is not your writing. Borrowing the zoom, with your own details, is how writers learn from mentor texts.

pool.prompt: Which setting detail builds a calm, safe mood?
choices: A warm fire crackles while rain taps on the window.
Footsteps creak on the stairs above.
The lights flicker and go out.
pool.hint: Which one would make you feel cosy?
pool.explain: A warm fire with rain outside feels safe and calm. The other two make the reader uneasy.

pool.prompt: Your plan says only: 1. Jay goes to camp. 2. He gets lost. 3. He is found. What is missing?
choices: Nothing, a plan is just the plot
Notes on how to show Jay and the setting's mood
Ten more events
pool.hint: A plan is more than what happens.
pool.explain: A list of events is a plot, not a full plan. Add notes on how Jay acts, speaks and thinks, and setting details for the mood you want.

pool.prompt: A setting has {n} details. Which order builds suspense like a camera zoom?
choices: Start close, then go wide
Start wide, then move closer each time
Put the details in any order
pool.explain: Start wide so the reader knows where they are, then move closer with each detail. The close-up at the end makes the reader lean in.

visual.caption: Plan notes: does each one show it or tell it? Drag each note, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: She chews her pencil and stares at the clock
Rain drums on the tin roof
“Go on, then,” he said, not looking up

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort telling from showing, read a mentor text like a writer, plan a character and a setting mood, and borrow the author's zoom.
